original_interpretation: The official WSTS product taxonomy groups semiconductors into discretes, optoelectronics, sensors and actuators, and integrated circuits, with ICs split into analog, micro (MPU, MCU, DSP), logic and memory (DRAM, SRAM, flash and others).
evidence_found: "3.1. Discretes ... 3.2. Optoelectronics ... 3.3. Sensors and Actuators ... 3.4. Integrated Circuits (3.4.1 Analog, 3.4.2 MOS Micro, 3.4.3 Total Logic, 3.4.4 MOS Memory)" (contents); "three subcategories, i.e. MOS Microprocessor (MPU) (code P1), MOS Microcontroller (MCU) (code P2), and Digital Signal Processor (DSP) (code P4)"; "DRAM (M1) SRAM (M2) Mask Programmable ROM & EPROM (M8) Flash Memory (M7) Other Memory (M6)" (sec. 3.4.4)
notes: Document is 'Product Classification 2021, Issue 1 - Date: 10 December 2020' (applies to 2021 reporting). Memory also lists Mask ROM & EPROM (M8), covered by 'others'. Newer annual WSTS classifications were not opened; the top-level structure is unchanged in WSTS 2025 press releases (Logic, Memory, Microprocessors, Analog, Sensors, Discretes).

original_interpretation: In front-end manufacturing, specialized facilities called fabs print nanometer-scale integrated circuits from the chip design into silicon wafers.
evidence_found: "Highly specialized semiconductor manufacturing facilities, typically called “fabs”, print the nanometer-scale integrated circuits from the chip design into silicon wafers." (BCG/SIA 2021, Wafer fabrication section, p. 16)

original_interpretation: The back-end stage converts the silicon wafers produced by fabs into finished chips ready to be assembled into electronic devices.
evidence_found: "This stage involves converting the silicon wafers produced by the fabs into finished chips that are ready to be assembled into electronic devices." (Assembly, packaging & testing section, p. 19)

original_interpretation: Depending on the product, wafer manufacturing involves roughly 400 to 1,400 process steps.
evidence_found: "Depending on the specific product, there are 400 to 1,400 steps in the overall manufacturing process semiconductor wafers." (p. 16)
notes: Source text literally reads 'manufacturing process semiconductor wafers' (missing 'of'); the researcher's bracketed [of] is a fair repair.

original_interpretation: The average time to fabricate finished semiconductor wafers (cycle time) is about 12 weeks.
evidence_found: "The average time to fabricate finished semiconductor wafers, known as the cycle time, is about 12 weeks, but it can take up to 14-20 weeks to complete for advanced processes." (p. 16)
notes: Claim omits the source's own caveat that advanced processes take 14-20 weeks. The same report (p. 20) also says the process 'involves hundreds of steps over one to two months', which is internally inconsistent with 12 weeks; atlas text should cite 12 weeks as an average and add the 14-20 week range for leading-edge.

original_interpretation: In lithography, the circuit patterns from the design are mapped onto a glass plate called a photomask, and ultraviolet light transfers the pattern to photoresist on the wafer.
evidence_found: "The integrated circuit patterns specified in the design are mapped onto a glass plate called a photomask. An ultraviolet (UV) light is applied to transfer the patterns to the photoresist material coating on the wafer surface." (Exhibit 6, step 2 Lithography, p. 17)

original_interpretation: BCG/SIA state that EUV lithography equipment is required to manufacture chips at 7 nanometers and below.
evidence_found: "Advanced lithography equipment, specifically those that harness Extreme Ultra-Violet (EUV) technology are required to manufacture chips at 7 nanometers and below. A single EUV machine can cost $150 million." (p. 20). Contra: TSMC: "In 2018, TSMC became the first foundry to start 7nm FinFET (N7) volume production"; N7+ (2019) was "the industry's first commercially available Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography technology".
correction: The attribution is accurate, but the statement itself is too strong. TSMC's first-generation 7nm (N7) entered volume production in 2018 using 193nm immersion DUV with multi-patterning. EUV only entered foundry volume production with N7+ in 2019. EUV became necessary in practice from 5nm-class nodes, not at 7nm. Do not present 'EUV is required at 7nm' as fact.
notes: See the new TSMC claims and the contradiction record in this batch. WikiChip (tier 3) also states 'For N7, TSMC continued to use deep ultraviolet (DUV) 193 nm ArF Immersion lithography.'

original_interpretation: Chip design accounted for about 53% of semiconductor industry value added and 65% of industry R&D (BCG/SIA estimate, 2019 data).
evidence_found: Body text: "Design activity is largely knowledge- and skill-intensive: it accounts for 65% of the total industry R&D and 53% of the value added." Same page, stage box: "Chip design 53% of industry R&D 13% of industry capex 50% of the value added"; Exhibit 4 (p. 13) gives the same 50%/13%/53% for design (p. 15)
correction: The quoted sentence exists, but the report contradicts itself. Its stage box and Exhibit 4 give design 53% of R&D and 50% of value added. Only those figures add up: R&D 53+13+3+3+9+1 plus 15-20% pre-competitive is about 100%, and value added 50+24+6+4+11+5 = 100%. With the body-text figures (65% and 53%) the totals come to more than 100%. Use 50% of value added and 53% of R&D (2019). See the superseding claim.
notes: The same internal inconsistency affects CLM-0476 and CLM-0477 (other units, same quote, sourced from the SIA-hosted copy SRC-0199). Contradiction record added.

original_interpretation: BCG/SIA estimated that total development cost of a state-of-the-art smartphone system-on-chip could exceed USD 1 billion.
evidence_found: "The total development cost of a new state-of-the-art system-on-chip for a flagship smartphone, including the specialized blocks required to process audio, video or provide high-speed wireless connectivity, could well exceed $1 billion." (p. 15)
notes: Hedged estimate ('could well exceed'); circa 2020; source gives no method. Same passage: derivatives / mature-node chips cost $20m-$200m to develop.

original_interpretation: EDA companies supply software and services used to design chips, and core IP suppliers license reusable component designs that design firms incorporate into their chip layouts.
evidence_found: "electronic design automation (EDA) companies provide sophisticated software and services to support designing semiconductors"; "Core IP suppliers license reusable components designs – commonly called “IP blocks” or “IPs” – with a defined interface and functionality to design firms to incorporate into their chip layouts." (p. 19)

original_interpretation: About 90% of advanced logic manufacturing capacity below 10 nm was located in Taiwan (BCG estimate, circa 2019-2020).
evidence_found: "East Asia + China concentrate ~75% of the wafer fabrication capacity; in particular, ~90% of advanced logic capacity <10 nm is located in Taiwan" with chart "BREAKDOWN OF THE GLOBAL WAFER FABRICATION CAPACITY BY REGION, 2019 (%)" showing 92% (deck p. 5, dated April 6, 2021). Newer: SIA/BCG May 2024, Exhibit 6, Logic <10 nm 2022: 69% / 31% / 0%.
correction: Accurate for 2019 (the chart shows 92%, rounded to ~90% in the slide title), but out of date. SIA/BCG's May 2024 'Emerging Resilience' report puts Taiwan at 69% and South Korea at 31% of <10nm logic capacity in 2022, with the US at 0%. It forecasts Taiwan at 47% in 2032. The 2024 study counted only fabs above 5K wspm and 8-inch or larger, excluding R&D fabs, so part of the drop may come from the change in method. See the superseding claim.
notes: Period is CY2019 (chart label), not 'circa 2019-2020'.

original_interpretation: EUV lithography uses light with a wavelength of 13.5 nm.
evidence_found: ASML: "prints microchips using light with a wavelength of just 13.5 nm – almost x-ray range" (EUV systems page, intro); imec: "Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography uses light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers, much shorter than the deep ultraviolet light previously used." (Lithography page, 'Extreme UV')

original_interpretation: EUV light is generated by a CO2 laser firing two pulses at a fast-moving drop of tin, vaporizing it.
evidence_found: "To generate EUV light, a CO2 laser fires two separate laser pulses at a fast-moving drop of tin. This vaporizes the tin and creates EUV light. It does this up to 50,000 times per second." (ASML EUV page, 'How does EUV work?' interactive, Light source)
notes: Text is in the interactive hotspot module (seen in the rendered DOM via browser), not in the static page text.

original_interpretation: Because EUV light is absorbed by everything including air, EUV systems use multilayer mirrors instead of lenses and keep the whole light path in high vacuum.
evidence_found: "EUV systems use several multilayer mirrors instead of lenses to guide the EUV light to the wafer, shrinking the reticle pattern by a factor of four."; "EUV light is absorbed by everything, even air. So the whole light path and everything the light interacts with – from source to wafer – must be in high vacuum." (ASML EUV page, interactive: Optical column; Vacuum chamber)

original_interpretation: ASML's NXE EUV systems have a numerical aperture of 0.33 and print features with a resolution of 13 nm.
evidence_found: "they have a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.33. These systems print microchip features with a resolution of 13 nm, which is unreachable with deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography." (ASML EUV page, NXE systems)

original_interpretation: ASML's High-NA EXE EUV systems have a numerical aperture of 0.55 and print with a resolution of 8 nm.
evidence_found: "With an (NA) of 0.55, their innovative new optics use our novel 13.5 nm EUV light source to provide higher contrast and print with a resolution of just 8 nm." (EUV page, EXE systems); "we've increased the NA from 0.33 in our NXE systems to 0.55 in EXE systems" (ASML, 25 Jan 2024, section 1)
notes: The EUV product page still says 'The EXE platform will support high-volume chip manufacturing in 2025–2026' (stale text, not part of this claim).

original_interpretation: High-NA EUV optics demagnify the mask pattern 4x in one direction and 8x in the other (anamorphic optics) to keep compatibility with existing reticles.
evidence_found: "Instead, the EXE uses an ingenious design: anamorphic optics. Rather than uniformly shrinking the pattern being printed, the system's mirrors demagnify it by 4x in one direction and 8x in the other. ... allowing chipmakers to continue using traditionally sized reticles." (ASML, 25 Jan 2024, section 1)
notes: The source gives two reasons: a lower angle of incidence on the reticle (reflectivity), and keeping standard-size reticles. Because of this, EXE exposure fields are half the size of NXE fields. In September 2026 Intel and ASML were promoting a move to 6x12-inch masks for High NA, so 'compatibility with existing reticles' may become less central.

original_interpretation: ASML shipped the first modules of the first High-NA EUV system to Intel in December 2023.
evidence_found: "After a decade of R&D, ASML shipped the first modules of the first High NA EUV lithography system to Intel in December 2023. The TWINSCAN EXE:5000 represents a significant step forward" (ASML story, Christine Middleton, January 25, 2024, para 1)

original_interpretation: The smallest printable feature (critical dimension) follows the Rayleigh criterion CD = k1 x wavelength / NA, with a physical limit of k1 = 0.25.
evidence_found: "CD = k1 • λ / NA"; "k1 (or the k1 factor) is a coefficient that depends on many factors related to the chip manufacturing process. The physical limit lithography is k1 = 0.25." (ASML, The Rayleigh criterion)
notes: k1 = 0.25 is the single-exposure physical limit; multi-patterning gets around it in effect. ASML states it without that nuance.

original_interpretation: ASML states that the microchip manufacturing process involves hundreds of steps and can take up to four months from design to mass production.
evidence_found: "The microchip manufacturing process involves hundreds of steps and can take up to four months from design to mass production." (ASML, How microchips are made, opening paragraph)
notes: ASML is not consistent here: its 'Six crucial steps' story (SRC-0159) says 'consists of thousands of steps and can take more than three months from design to production'. BCG/SIA (SRC-0153) gives 400-1,400 steps. Treat these as loose, popular figures.

original_interpretation: Modern chips can have up to 100 layers, all of which must align on top of each other with nanometer precision.
evidence_found: "Modern chips can have up to 100 layers, which all need to align on top of each other with nanometer precision (called 'overlay')." (ASML, How microchips are made, 'Tiny skyscrapers')
notes: Popular-education page from an equipment maker; the figure is loose, and ASML's own 'Six crucial steps' story says some 3D NAND designs reach 'up to 175 layers'. Those are memory-cell layers, which are a different measure from patterned layers. claim_type 'fact' is generous; treat as a statement by ASML.

original_interpretation: Silicon wafers are sliced from a highly purified silicon bar called an ingot and polished to extreme smoothness.
evidence_found: "Wafers are sliced from a salami-shaped bar of 99.99% pure silicon (known as an 'ingot') and polished to extreme smoothness." (ASML, Six crucial steps, Deposition section, updated October 4, 2023)
notes: The claim rightly leaves out ASML's '99.99%' figure. Electronic-grade silicon is far purer than that, so do not quote it.

original_interpretation: Chipmaking repeats a loop of deposition, photoresist coating, lithography, etching and ion implantation, and a chip goes through this process hundreds of times.
evidence_found: "Thin films of conducting, isolating or semiconducting materials ... are deposited on the wafer"; "The wafer is then covered with a light-sensitive coating called 'photoresist'"; "the wafer may be bombarded with positive or negative ions"; "And each microchip goes through this process hundreds of times before it becomes part of a device." (ASML, Six crucial steps)
notes: BCG/SIA (SRC-0153 p. 17) also says the coat-lithography-etch-doping steps 'are repeated hundreds of times'.

original_interpretation: Immersion DUV lithography places a layer of water between the lithography system's optics and the silicon wafer.
evidence_found: Image caption/alt on ASML DUV page: "A close-up picture of a layer of water between our lithography system's optics and a silicon wafer." ASML story (2 Aug 2023): "adding a layer of purified water under the lens to sharpen the resolution".
notes: On SRC-0160 the wording appears only as image alt text and a link teaser, not in the body text. The fuller primary statement is in ASML's 'How immersion lithography saved Moore's Law' (https://www.asml.com/en/company/stories/2023/how-immersion-lithography-saved-moores-law), which supports the claim.

original_interpretation: ASML expects its High-NA EXE platform to start supporting high-volume manufacturing in 2027.
evidence_found: AR 2025 p. 16: "We expect our TWINSCAN EXE platform to start supporting high-volume manufacturing in 2027." Newer: ASML PR 15 Jul 2026: "Intel Foundry has entered high-volume manufacturing for a subset of Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 3 processors ... using ASML's EXE High NA EUV technology"
correction: Accurate as ASML's early-2026 expectation, but overtaken by events. On 15 July 2026 ASML reported that Intel Foundry had entered high-volume manufacturing with High NA EUV on select Intel 18A layers, for a subset of Panther Lake (see CLM-1707). On 8 September 2026 Intel and ASML said High NA 'continues to be used in high-volume manufacturing production at Intel Foundry today'. Broader multi-customer HVM is still ahead.
notes: The ASML EUV product page (SRC-0155) still says '2025–2026', which shows ASML's HVM timing statements have moved over time.

original_interpretation: In 2025 ASML recognized revenue for four High-NA (0.55 NA) EUV systems shipped to customers' R&D facilities.
evidence_found: "For EUV 0.55 NA, we recognized revenue for four systems that were shipped to customers' R&D facilities." (ASML Annual Report 2025, 'What it means for ASML', p. 20)
notes: Location is printed page 20, not p. 21. Consistent with CLM-1640 (4 EXE systems, EUR 1,156.9m in 2025).

original_interpretation: By the end of 2025, ASML's customers had run more than 400,000 wafers on High-NA EUV systems.
evidence_found: "In terms of High NA EUV, the dynamics around productivity, imaging and overlay performance are very positive. By the end of the year, our customers had run more than 400,000 wafers on High NA EUV systems." (ASML AR 2025, Q&A with the CEO, p. 8)
notes: Correct as a cumulative figure to end-2025. Newer: in September 2026 Intel Foundry and ASML cited 'more than one million wafers processed to date' on High NA (new claim in this batch). That figure seems to cover Intel Foundry, so the two are not strictly comparable.

original_interpretation: ASML states it is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV lithography systems.
evidence_found: "ASML is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV lithography systems. Our EUV product roadmap is intended to drive affordable scaling to 2030 and beyond." (ASML AR 2025, p. 16)
notes: Correctly typed as reported_claim. ZEISS says the same (CLM-1680). No contrary evidence found as of 2026-10.

original_interpretation: ASML reported about 5,100 suppliers in total in its 2025 annual report, and names Carl Zeiss SMT as strategic partner for High-NA projection optics.
evidence_found: "5,100 Total number of suppliers" (AR 2025 at-a-glance, p. 4; p. 41: "5,100 Total number of suppliers 2024: 5,150"); "improved projection optics, developed in cooperation with our strategic partner Carl Zeiss SMT" (re TWINSCAN EXE:5200B, p. 16)
notes: This claim joins two facts and should be split. The supplier count was 5,150 in 2024. P. 68 adds that Carl Zeiss SMT is ASML's 'sole supplier' of optics under an 'exclusive arrangement' (see CLM-1665).

original_interpretation: Process node names such as '7 nm' or '3 nm' no longer refer to any specific physical measurement on the chip, although historically they corresponded to transistor feature lengths.
evidence_found: "For decades, the process “node” name corresponded to the actual length of certain physical transistor features."; "Today, the various naming and numbering schemes used across the industry no longer refer to any specific measurement" (Intel Accelerated fact sheet, 26 Jul 2021, p. 3)
notes: This is Intel's statement, made while it was renaming its own nodes. Footnote 2 adds that Intel's node numbers 'do not represent the actual dimension of any physical feature'. Typing it as 'fact' is acceptable since it is widely accepted, but the source is a company document.

original_interpretation: Intel describes RibbonFET as its gate-all-around transistor and its first new transistor architecture since it introduced FinFETs in 2011.
evidence_found: "RibbonFET, Intel's implementation of a gate-all-around transistor, is the company's first new transistor architecture since it pioneered FinFETs in 2011" (Intel Accelerated fact sheet, p. 2, Intel 20A)

original_interpretation: Intel's PowerVia is a backside power delivery technique that removes the need to route power on the front side of the wafer.
evidence_found: "PowerVia is Intel's unique, industry-first implementation of backside power delivery – eliminating the need for power routing on the front side of the wafer and providing optimized signal routing while reducing droop and lowering noise." (Intel Accelerated fact sheet, p. 2)
notes: The 2021 fact sheet tied PowerVia to Intel 20A ('expected to ramp in 2024') and carries forward-looking disclaimers. 'Industry-first' is marketing. Whether 20A shipped was not checked here.
